references.text: Jacob sets up the stone as a pillar (מַצֵּבָה) and pours oil over it – the direct action that verse 22 refers back to.
Jacob builds an altar in Bethel and calls the place El-Bethel, thus fulfilling the promise from Genesis 28:22 that the stone would become God's house.
Jacob sets up a pillar of stone at the place where God spoke with him in Bethel, linking back to the original pillar in Genesis 28:18 and the promise in verse 22.
God identifies Himself as the God of Bethel, where Jacob anointed a pillar and made a vow – a direct reference to the event in Genesis 28:18-22.
Abraham gives a tenth to Melchizedek – the first occurrence of tithing in the Bible and a precursor to Jacob's promise to give a tenth to God.
The law on tithing: all tithes of the land belong to the Lord. Jacob's promise of tithing in Genesis 28:22 anticipates this legislation.
The command to give a tenth of everything you harvest – a codification of the tithe practice that Jacob promised in Genesis 28:22.
Hebrews mentions Abraham's tithe to Melchizedek, which together with Genesis 14:20 shows the early practice of tithing that Jacob continues in his vow.
Both verses establish a theological connection between a physical memorial or altar and God's promise to meet His people where His name is remembered.
The verses illuminate each other as precursor and fulfillment of the concept 'God's house', from Jacob's pillar to the prophesied eternal dwelling among His people.
Both verses deal with the theological dynamic between making vows to God and fulfilling them through thank offerings and tithes.
The verses link Jacob's personal consecration of the stone as 'God's house' with God's later selection and consecration of the temple forever.
The verses illuminate each other by tracing the development of 'God's house' from Jacob's local memorial to the prophesied house of prayer for all peoples.
Both verses illustrate the use of stones as a living memorial and sign to future generations about God's actions.
The verses connect the recognition of a place as 'God's house' with the necessary attitude of reverence at the entrance to the holy.
